explained.headline: Ukraine and Russia begin Oleshky ceasefire

happened.text: Russia and Ukraine began a localized ceasefire early Tuesday to allow humanitarian aid into the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in southern Ukraine.
Both sides confirmed that the truce took effect following an agreement brokered by United States first lady Melania Trump.
While the truce began, Russian missile attacks continued elsewhere in Ukraine, hitting the capital Kyiv and damaging a bridge and subway infrastructure.

background.text: Oleshky lies across the Dnipro River from the Ukrainian-controlled city of Kherson and was captured by Russian troops during the first days of the full-scale invasion in February 2022.
Residents remaining in the town have faced severe shortages of food, water and medicine, with many trapped by mines and drone attacks.
The United States first lady previously became involved in humanitarian issues stemming from the war, writing a letter to Russian President Vladimir Putin in August 2025.

matters.text: Melania Trump stated that residents wishing to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination.

uncertain.text: It could not be independently verified whether fighting had decreased in the area.
Ukraine has accused Russia of preventing residents from leaving, an allegation that Moscow denies.

removed.text: The agreement is intended to allow civilian officials from both countries to visit residents, deliver doctors, food, drinking water and medicine, and open evacuation corridors.
why: The evidence qualifies these actions as expected, whereas the claim states them as intent.

removed.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stated that the continued attacks on Kyiv demonstrate that Russia desires only to kill and continue waging war.
why: The word 'only' was not used in the evidence quote.

removed.text: Neither side has provided details about who will monitor the ceasefire or how long it will last.
why: Evidence confirms these details are missing, but contradicts the claim that duration is unknown.

explained.headline: Jordan Strikes Militants in Syria Following Deadly Church Attack

happened.text: Jordan carried out airstrikes in southern Syria after determining that suspects linked to a deadly church attack were hiding there.
Syrian health officials stated that five people, including women, children and an elderly man, were killed in the strike in Daraa province.
Earlier on Monday, Jordanian security forces arrested three men in connection with the church shooting following a dawn shootout in an abandoned house.
In response to the Jordanian military action, Syria announced the closure of the Nassib border crossing.

background.text: The military actions followed a shooting at a funeral in a Greek Orthodox church in Karak that killed nine people.
King Abdullah II of Jordan, the country's monarch, had ordered an iron fist response against anyone attempting to divide the population.
Mazen al-Faraya serves as Jordan's interior minister.
Attacks on Christian minorities are very rare in Jordan, which is a stable Middle Eastern state and a close ally of the United States.

matters.text: Jordanian interior minister Mazen al-Faraya warned that further similar incidents could occur if extremist ways of thinking are not resolved.
Relatives of the church attack victims stated that the arrests of the suspects brought some relief to their immense grief.

uncertain.text: Jordan stated it had coordinated the strikes with the Syrian government, while Syria stated it had not been notified and launched its own investigation.
Jordanian authorities did not provide further details regarding the exact number of terrorists killed or wounded in the air raids.

removed.text: The closure of the Nassib border crossing suspended all passenger and commercial traffic in both directions.
No group claimed responsibility for the initial church attack, and officials noted the attackers were not tied to any organised group.
why: One source says no claim, but another notes officials identified them as 'takfiri' but not organized.

explained.headline: Brazil election won by Lula as Bolsonaro refuses to concede

happened.text: Left-wing incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva won the Brazilian presidential runoff election with 51.7% of the vote against Flavio Bolsonaro's 48.2%.
Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered Flavio Bolsonaro to surrender his passports and banned him from leaving the country.

background.text: Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva is the left-wing president of Brazil and a former union leader who has had famously strained relations with United States governments.

matters.text: Brazil's Liberal Party acknowledged Lula's election victory despite the challenger's refusal to concede.
US President Donald Trump remarked that the vote looked terrible and rigged while simultaneously stating that he likes Lula.

uncertain.text: It remains unclear whether Flavio Bolsonaro will continue to resist the election outcome and attempt to encourage protests.
Neither the Supreme Court nor federal police immediately confirmed the reported passport surrender ruling to media.

explained.headline: Two Men Charged Under National Security Act After RAF Fairford Incident

happened.text: British prosecutors stated that two men had been charged under the National Security Act following a September incident near the RAF Fairford airbase in England.
Mohmed Abdulkarim was charged with assisting a foreign intelligence service, while Nouman Essghir was charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the United Kingdom.
Armed police and bomb-disposal experts responded to the base on September 27, evacuating dozens of residents to search the rural area for explosives.

background.text: RAF Fairford is an airbase in Gloucestershire, southwestern England, that had been used by United States bombers to carry out strikes on Iran this year.
Britain previously stated there were 20 credible Iranian-backed threats to kill or kidnap individuals based in the UK last year, and banned support for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in July.

matters.text: Counterterrorism police chief Laurence Taylor said investigators believed the foreign intelligence service involved was Iran, and British Prime Minister Andy Burnham stated the activity was likely coordinated in Iran.
United States bombers were withdrawn from the Fairford airbase on security grounds shortly after the arrests.

uncertain.text: Six other men who were arrested during the course of the investigation remain on police bail while enquiries continue.
